name: Shadow AI in Legal Teams
title: Shadow AI in Legal Teams
answer: Shadow AI in legal teams covers any AI tool or model that lawyers, paralegals, or legal operations staff use without formal approval from the firm's IT, security, or compliance function. It typically includes consumer chatbots for drafting, free transcription services for client meetings, and browser extensions that summarize documents. The scope also extends to sanctioned tools used in unsanctioned ways, such as pasting privileged material into a public model or connecting a firm account to an unvetted plugin. Because legal work involves client confidences and attorney-client privilege, shadow AI is treated as a data governance problem first and a productivity question second.

sections.body: Shadow AI in legal teams covers any AI tool or model that lawyers, paralegals, or legal operations staff use without formal approval from the firm's IT, security, or compliance function. It typically includes consumer chatbots for drafting, free transcription services for client meetings, and browser extensions that summarize documents. The scope also extends to sanctioned tools used in unsanctioned ways, such as pasting privileged material into a public model or connecting a firm account to an unvetted plugin. Because legal work involves client confidences and attorney-client privilege, shadow AI is treated as a data governance problem first and a productivity question second.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Shadow AI runs on whatever devices and accounts staff already have: personal phones, web browsers, free tiers of cloud services, and sometimes firm-issued laptops with local models. It often bypasses the firm's virtual private network, single sign-on, and data loss prevention controls because the user logs in with a personal email or uses a consumer API key. The infrastructure is therefore fragmented: no central logging, no retention policy, no e-discovery hold, and no way for the firm to know which prompts or documents left its perimeter. In some cases, shadow AI runs inside sanctioned platforms through unapproved integrations, which makes it harder to detect than a standalone app.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Legal professionals use shadow AI for summarization, first drafts, redlining, legal research, translation, e-discovery culling, and client intake. The work is done ad hoc, often by copying text into a chat window or uploading files to a web service, then pasting the output back into a matter file. There is no review protocol tied to the tool, no prompt log, and no check against the firm's conflicts or confidentiality rules. Because the user is not a machine learning engineer, they may not know whether the model retains inputs, trains on them, or shares them with third parties. The method is essentially manual and invisible to the firm's quality control.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Shadow AI weakens provenance because the firm cannot show who generated a passage, with what tool, under what prompt, or on what date. Rights are unclear: the model's output may incorporate third-party copyrighted material, and the firm may have no license to use it in client work. The main risks are waiver of attorney-client privilege, breach of confidentiality, and loss of control over data retention and deletion. Regulatory exposure follows from data protection and professional conduct rules that require competent supervision of technology. Without logs or access controls, the firm cannot demonstrate that it met its duty of technological competence.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Shadow AI in legal teams is moving toward detection and enablement rather than outright prohibition. Firms are beginning to deploy network monitoring, browser extensions, and cloud access security brokers to find unsanctioned AI use, then route users to approved tools with equivalent features. The likely endpoint is a managed AI catalog with per-matter permissions, prompt logging, and data residency controls, so that legal staff can use generative AI without leaving the firm's security boundary. Some teams are also piloting private instances of large language models inside the firm's own cloud tenant, which reduces the incentive to use consumer tools. Over time, shadow AI may become less of a security audit problem and more of a change management and training challenge.
